newsitem.title: INDIA: Congress divided on support to Indian government.
newsitem.headline: Congress divided on support to Indian government.

text.p: India's Congress party chose Sitaram Kesri as its new parliamentary leader on Friday and the veteran politician quickly reiterated support for the country's minority government.
But the apparent unanimity on his appointment was overshadowed by divisions over the party's support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Congress lawmakers elected Kesri unopposed to replace former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao as the head of the Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP), party officials said.

Kesri wasted no time in seeking to dispel nagging rumours that a reinvigorated Congress, which suffered its worst ever defeat in general elections last year, would set out to challenge Deve Gowda's United Front minority coalition.
"All this talk about our withdrawing support to the United Front is wrong. It is a ploy to frighten you," Kesri told the CPP.
But Kesri's senior party colleagues soon dismissed the remarks.
"It was a tactical comment," said a key Kesri aide.
"I won't give the government six months. The Congress will form its own government soon, be sure of that," a former minister said.
Deve Gowda's centre-left minority coalition needs Congress' support to survive a challenge from the Hindu nationalist opposition in the lower house of parliament.

Kesri, who became Congress party president in September when Rao stepped down under pressure, beat back a youthful challenge from former cabinet minister Rajesh Pilot, who had earlier won backing from Rao loyalists.
"The consensus is in favour of Sitaram Kesri," former finance minister Manmohan Singh told a meeting of the CPP.
Rao, who was prime minister from 1991 until last May and spearheaded a drive to open up India's economy, quit under pressure as CPP leader last month.
Kesri complained the reforms had not reached the poor.
Without naming Rao, he said: "Whenever the party has strayed from Mahatma Gandhi's path of caring for the poor, it has faced trouble."
He said: "If today we have to suffer the spectacle of a 13-party hotchpotch of a government, we have only oursleves to blame.
"But do not worry too much. Yours is a very strong party, and the only viable force in the country. It won't take long for you to get back your former glory."
Congress, which has led India for all but four years since independence in 1947, suffered its worst-ever defeat in general elections last April and May.

Rao stepped down as Congress party president in September after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court to face criminal cheating charges. Kesri was named to succeed Rao at the head of India's oldest party.

The case is one of three criminal proceedings involving the taciturn, 75-year-old Rao, who claims he is innocent of the charges which, in each of the three cases, carry a maximum penalty of seven years in jail.
Rao had clung to his CPP post despite mounting opposition from Congress members keen to revamp the party's tarnished image.
But Rao bowed to the inevitable as supporters deserted him in the face of a campaign to overhaul the party's leadership, badly hit by corruption scandals.
"I have the twin objective of implementing Mahatma Gandhi's ideals and to weed out corruption," Kesri said to thunderous applause.
